verdicts.evidence: The local import binds os to the os module, and the if condition directly tests os.name (f1:12-13, s1).
The condition compares os.name to the literal nt with equality, and the guarded block is its then arm without any intervening negation (s1, s2).
The test reads the operating-system identifier os.name, so os is the appropriate category (s1).
The region has one enclosing decision, os.name == nt, with no additional Boolean conditions; c1 alone satisfies the then branch and its minimum is one (s1-s3).
In the supplied derived code, the OS condition enables the request and execution of its response; there is no alternative payload branch (f2:13-18).
Equality with nt activates the guarded execution on that OS rather than testing for an analysis environment (s1, f2:13-16).
The OS check restricts downloading and executing the response to nt, while the normal installer call follows outside the condition; this supports targeting (f2:13-18).

The cited region in f1 executes a decrypted value, whereas both sinks are in the supplied derived f2; the packet supplies no derivation mapping proving that decrypted value reaches those sinks (s3-s5). Within f2 itself, both calls are directly inside the matching then arm.

Both sinks in f2 occur only inside its OS conditional, but the claimed guard and region refer to f1's encrypted execution with no supplied derivation mapping to f2 (s2-s5). This leaves exclusivity through the cited original gate unproved.

In f2, requests is imported directly and requests.get retrieves response text; that text passes through two replacements into built-in exec, supporting download and execution of downloaded code (f2:14-16, s4-s5).
